items.prompt: Write the opening of a story set during a power cut on a stormy night. Describe what your character sees, hears and feels.

criteria.label: Sets the scene using sight, sound or touch
Uses at least one simile or metaphor
Introduces a character and a problem
Uses paragraphs and different sentence openings
Uses capital letters, full stops and speech marks correctly

planning: Who is your main character, and where are they?
What can they hear, see and feel in the dark?
What problem or surprise could start the story?
items.model:
The lights went out at exactly eight o’clock. One moment Nisa was finishing her maths homework, and the next the kitchen was as black as the inside of a pocket. Outside, the rain drummed on the roof like a hundred impatient fingers.

“Ibu?” she called. No answer. Her mother had gone next door to borrow some sugar.

Nisa felt along the table until her fingers found the cold metal of the torch. She pressed the switch. Nothing.

Then she heard it: a slow scratching at the back door. Scritch. Scritch. Scritch.

She held her breath. Somewhere outside, the cat she had forgotten to let in gave a very offended meow.
hints: Start at the exact moment the lights go out.
Use your senses: what can your character hear and feel in the dark?
items.explanation: A strong story opening sets the scene, introduces a character and hints at a problem, so the reader wants to find out what happens next.

items.prompt: Write a letter persuading your head teacher to start a book swap. Pupils could exchange books they have finished.

criteria.label: Uses the layout of a formal letter: greeting, paragraphs and sign-off
States the request clearly in the first paragraph
Gives at least three reasons with examples or facts
Answers a possible argument against the idea
Uses a polite, formal tone with no slang

planning: What exactly are you asking for?
What are your three best reasons? Add an example to each one.
What might someone say against the idea, and how would you answer?
How will you end the letter politely?
items.model:
Dear Mrs Lestari,

I am writing to ask you to start a book swap in our school library.

First, many pupils have books at home that they have already finished. In my class alone, we counted 64. A book swap would let us exchange them for free, so everyone gets something new to read.

Secondly, a book swap would encourage pupils who do not usually read. When a friend recommends a book, it is much more exciting to try it.

Some people may worry that books will get lost. However, the library monitors could keep a simple record of every swap.

I would be very grateful if you could discuss this idea with the teachers.

Yours sincerely,

Bima Santoso, Class 5A
hints: Say exactly what you want in your first sentence.
Think about what a teacher might worry about, and answer that worry.
items.explanation: A persuasive letter states its request clearly, gives reasons with evidence, answers an objection and ends politely.

items.prompt: Write a short biography of someone you admire. It could be a family member or a famous person. Write in the third person and in time order.

criteria.label: Written in the third person (he, she or they)
Events are in time order, with dates or time phrases
Uses a new paragraph for each part of the person’s life
Includes interesting facts or achievements
Ends by explaining why the person matters
Spelling and punctuation are correct

planning: When and where was the person born?
What were the most important events in their life, in order?
What are they best known for?
Why do you admire them?
items.model:
Siti Aminah was born in 1958 in a small village near Kediri. She was the oldest of six children, so she often looked after her brothers and sisters while her parents worked in the fields.

When she was twelve, she began helping at her aunt’s sewing stall in the market. By the age of twenty, she had saved enough money to buy her own sewing machine.

In 1985, she opened a small tailor’s shop. Over the next thirty years, she made school uniforms for thousands of children and taught more than twenty young people to sew.

Today, my grandmother still sews every morning. I admire her because she built her business from nothing and always helped others to learn.
hints: If you are writing about a family member, ask them questions first.
Use time phrases such as when she was ten, later and today.
items.explanation: A biography tells the story of a real person’s life in time order, in the third person, with facts and dates.

items.prompt: Write an explanation of how something works or happens, such as how rain forms or how a bicycle moves. Use a title, an introduction and cause and effect words.

criteria.label: Has a clear title and an introduction
Explains the steps in a logical order
Uses cause and effect words such as because, so and as a result
Uses technical words correctly
Written in the present tense in a formal style
Ends with a short sentence that sums up

planning: What will you explain, and who is your reader?
What happens first, next and last?
Which words will show cause and effect?
Which technical words will you need to use and explain?
items.model:
How Rain Forms

Rain is part of the water cycle, the journey that water makes again and again between the land, the sea and the sky.

First, the sun heats water in seas, lakes and rivers. As a result, some of the water evaporates and becomes water vapour, an invisible gas that rises into the air.

Higher up, the air is cooler, so the water vapour condenses into tiny droplets. Millions of these droplets together form clouds.

Inside the clouds, droplets bump into each other and join to make bigger drops. When the drops become too heavy to float, they fall as rain.

The rain flows into rivers and back to the sea, and the cycle begins again.
hints: Choose something you understand well, so that you can explain it clearly.
Imagine your reader knows nothing about the topic. What do they need to know first?
items.explanation: An explanation text tells the reader how or why something happens, step by step, using cause and effect words.

items.prompt: Write a news report about an exciting event at your school, such as a sports day or a science fair. Include a headline, the main facts and a quotation.

criteria.label: Has a short, catchy headline
The first paragraph says who, what, where and when
Includes at least one quotation in speech marks
Written in the past tense and the third person
Ends with what will happen next
Punctuation is correct, including speech marks

planning: What happened, who was involved, when and where?
Why was it important or unusual?
What did someone who was there say?
What will happen next?
items.model:
Paper Bridge Holds 2 Kilograms

By Dani Prakoso

A paper bridge built by three Class 5 pupils held 2 kilograms of rice at the SD Harapan Science Fair on Friday, beating fourteen other teams.

Lia, Joni and Mega spent two weeks testing folds and shapes before choosing a design made from rolled tubes of newspaper.

“We broke eleven bridges before this one,” said Lia, laughing. “The tubes made it much stronger.”

The judges praised the team for recording every test in a notebook.

The bridge will be displayed in the library until the end of term.
hints: Put the most important facts in your first sentence.
Imagine you asked someone who was there a question. What did they say?
items.explanation: A news report gives the most important facts first, uses quotations from people involved and is written in the past tense.

items.prompt: Continue this story and give it an ending. Use dialogue to show how the characters feel. When Fikri opened his lunch box, he found a folded note that was not from his mum.

criteria.label: The story follows on clearly from the opening
Has a clear problem and a satisfying ending
Uses dialogue that shows how the characters feel
Punctuates dialogue correctly, with a new line for each speaker
Uses precise verbs and some figurative language
Uses paragraphs to move the story on

planning: Who wrote the note, and what does it say?
What does Fikri decide to do?
What problem or surprise happens next?
How does the story end, and how has Fikri changed?
items.model:
When Fikri opened his lunch box, he found a folded note that was not from his mum. It said: Can you show me where the library is? From the new boy.

Fikri looked around. In the corner sat a thin boy with enormous glasses, staring hard at his shoes.

At break, Fikri walked over. “Did you write this?” he asked.

The boy turned as red as a chilli. “Sorry. I was too nervous to ask.”

“No problem,” said Fikri. “I’m going there now. What’s your name?”

“Leo. We just moved from Medan.”

They spent the whole of break among the shelves, arguing happily about dinosaurs. That evening, Fikri told his mum. “Next time,” she said, smiling, “I’ll pack a snack for Leo too.”
hints: Decide who wrote the note before you start writing.
Show feelings through what characters say and do, rather than naming the feeling.
items.explanation: A good story ending solves the problem in a way that makes sense, and dialogue helps the reader understand how the characters feel.

items.prompt: Which sentence would be the best opening for a persuasive letter to your head teacher?

options.why: This is too informal for a head teacher and does not say what you want.

options.text: I am writing to ask you to open the school library at lunchtime.

options.why: This does not tell the reader why you are writing.

options.text: Once upon a time, there was a library.
options.why: This is a story opening, not a letter opening.

hints: A letter to a head teacher should be polite and formal.
The first sentence should say clearly why you are writing.
Cross out any option that sounds like a story or a chat with a friend.
items.explanation: A persuasive letter should begin by stating its purpose clearly and politely: I am writing to ask you to...

items.prompt: Put the parts of a formal letter in order.
items: What you would like the reader to do
hints: A letter starts with information about the writer and ends with the writer’s name.
The greeting comes before the main part. The sign-off comes after it.
Start with what goes at the very top of the page.
items.explanation: A formal letter begins with your address, the date and a greeting. The body explains your purpose and reasons and ends with a request, then comes the sign-off and your name.

items.prompt: Which sentence belongs in an explanation text about volcanoes?

options.text: I think volcanoes are the scariest thing ever!
options.why: This is an opinion. Explanations give facts.

options.text: Once upon a time, a volcano woke up.
When pressure builds up under the ground, magma rises and bursts out through the crater.
Visit Mount Bromo for an amazing sunrise!
options.why: This is an advert, which tries to persuade.

hints: An explanation tells how or why something happens.
Look for facts and cause and effect, not opinions or stories.
Find the sentence that says what causes something to happen.
items.explanation: Explanations use facts and cause and effect. The correct sentence explains what makes a volcano erupt.

items.prompt: A biography is written in the third person. Which sentence is written in the third person?

options.text: I was born in Surabaya in 2015.
options.why: I shows the first person, used in an autobiography.

options.text: You were born in Surabaya in 2015.
She was born in Surabaya in 2015.
We were born in Surabaya in 2015.
options.why: We is the first person plural.

hints: The first person is I and we. The second person is you.
Third person words include he, she, they and people’s names.
Look at the first word of each sentence.
items.explanation: She is a third person pronoun. Biographies use he, she, they or the person’s name.
